query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: During cooling from the high-temperature BCC state, Al atoms rapidly diffuse and locally enrich to nucleate nanoscale B2-ordered precipitates; these B2 precipitates alter the local chemical potential landscape and act as a structural mediator that lowers the barrier to subsequent L12 (γ′) phase formation, thereby controlling which combination of B2, γ′ and residual BCC appears after thermal exposure.
generation.intervention: Cooling at controlled rates (e.g. 1 °C/s vs. 100 °C/s) from 1100 °C to 300 °C
generation.conditions: Al content ≥ 7 at %, cooling through 900–300 °C; applies when no external stresses are applied during cooling
generation.mechanism: Al clustering drives B2 nucleation, which in turn modifies local composition fields to favor L12 γ′ ordering at lower temperatures
generation.predicted_outcome: Slow-cooled specimens will show a higher volume fraction of B2 precipitates and subsequent γ′ precipitates, whereas rapid-quenched specimens remain largely single-phase BCC
generation.baseline: Rapid quench (>100 °C/s) from 1100 °C to room temperature expected to retain a homogeneous BCC without B2 or γ′
generation.boundary: Does not apply if cooling is interrupted above 900 °C or if Al < 7 at % (insufficient Al to form B2 clusters)
generation.uncertainty: Moderate – the exact volume fractions of B2 and γ′ and their size distributions are not known a priori

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples from the same batch, hold at 1100 °C, then cool one set at ~1 °C/s and the other at >100 °C/s to 300 °C. Characterize both by X-ray diffraction (to quantify B2 and γ′ peaks), transmission electron microscopy (to image precipitates), and differential scanning calorimetry (to detect ordering heat effects).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow-cooled samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in B2 volume fraction (and/or γ′ fraction) relative to the rapid-quenched baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
